analysis: The broad option covers central normative, political, metaphysical and mind questions directly through philosophy, with logic and rhetoric contributing argument methods. History, literary analysis, myth, archaeology and ancient democracy give context for intellectual traditions and their reception. These are complementary rather than specialist non-Western philosophy.

The practical option gives substantial weight to moral and political philosophy, rights and criminal, constitutional and EU law. Social movements, critical sociology and histories of gender provide material for applying questions about justice and institutions. Criminal Law follows the gateway in the later available autumn.

The theoretical option makes mind, cognition and language central. Philosophy of mind and agency and formal logic are supported by neuroscience, psycholinguistics, empirical research and machine learning. The methods support enquiry about cognition. They do not substitute for philosophy-of-science courses.

The three options differ qualitatively and exceed the minimum distinctness. The programme’s methods and thesis sequence and non-Western and philosophy-of-science depth remain explicit gaps. Option-specific contribution was checked against the current workbook; courses are paired only where their content or substantive method overlaps.
constructionStop: Three coherent, distinct options reach the programme limit.

HCBCOGN312.contribution: examines the psychological and neural processes of human language production and comprehension
HCBCOGN312.topics: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.
